editorial.headline: Licensing Intellectual Property: Nationally Open, PMA-Barred in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity turns non-copyright intellectual-property rights into royalty income—open nationally to full foreign ownership, yet barred from PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 77400 is the business of allowing another party to use non-copyright intellectual-property assets, or comparable products, in exchange for royalties or licence consideration paid to the owner or asset holder. Permission can take several commercial forms: reproduction, use within a later process or production, or the operation of a business under a franchise system. The present owner need not be the person who created the asset. It can therefore sit behind arrangements that make an asset usable by another enterprise without transferring ownership.

The activity includes operational leasing without an option for eligible intellectual-property products, together with receiving royalties or licence fees. The record identifies patented entities, trademarks and service marks, trade names, mineral-exploration rights, franchise agreements, internet domains, and rights in designed or developed board games. It also includes royalties or licence fees for the results of scientific research. The category is framed by the commercial permission and the fee stream attached to it, however varied the underlying asset may be.

Nationally, the investment position is unambiguous. The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, spanning the full range stated in the record. Its national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, so there is no national cap below full foreign ownership. For founders, that means the rights-and-royalties character of the business does not confine it to a particular listed scale, and the national setting permits a wholly foreign-owned PMA registration.

Bali changes the answer completely. For this activity, Bali's moratorium is decisive: a foreigner cannot register it there as PMA today. At the Besar scale, every scope is recorded as Low or Medium-Low risk, placing the activity within Bali's permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for those risk levels. This is not a reduction of the national 100% ceiling or a case-by-case caution; it is a provincial bar under the moratorium dated 13 May 2026. National openness remains relevant outside Bali, but within Bali the moratorium controls the registration outcome.
